## Abstract

## Introduction:

This study explores the interplay between United States (US) state-level legislation and the well-being of transgender individuals of color against the backdrop of state legislature political ideology in 2024.

## Methods

Using a polytomous latent class analysis, we drew from the Movement Advancement Project’s Gender Identity Tally and a structural racism legal database to categorize states based on policies affecting transgender rights and structural racism.

## Results

Our study identifies three state classes: Mostly Protective, Mixed, and Mostly Harmful. Key findings indicate state legislatures with more liberal ideologies tend to enact protective policies, and ideological diversity within state legislatures, regardless of political ideology, does not guarantee safeguards for trans people of color.

## Conclusion and Policy Implications:

This research advocates for more targeted and inclusive legislative frameworks to enhance health equity and rights for transgender individuals of color. Our work contributes to a deeper understanding of how political environments shape health, calling for policies that address racial and gender experiences comprehensively.

## 1. Introduction

In the United States (US), policies – both exclusionary and inclusive – create different sociopolitical contexts that shape state-dependent health outcomes that are both gendered and racialized.(Kline et al., 2023) For this study, we use the word “trans” to refer to both transgender and nonbinary individuals. Trans individuals of color in the US live in political contexts that impact their health on the axes of race/ethnicity, transgender identity, and the intersection of the two. Some studies find that trans individuals who are Black or Latiné are more likely to identify as trans than white adults.(Flores et al., 2016; Pew Research Center, 2023) Trans individuals of color are differentially impacted by transgenderrelated policies than their white counterparts, with some studies positing that specific policies (e.g., private health insurance) have a protective effect on self-rated health only for white transgender individuals.(King et al., 2024) Studies related to transgender health driven by state-level policy exposures fail to consider how structurally racist policies in these same states may contribute to a more robust

definition and conceptualizing of policy environments that impact transgender individuals of color. This study creates a typology of US states using indicators of structural racism and trans-related policies to create a different way of defining protective, harmful, and mixed policy environments. Further, we examine how political ideology and ideological diversity within state legislatures are associated with protectiveness using our typology for trans individuals of color.

A rise of state-level anti-trans bills in the US occurred between 2015 and 2024, with the most marked inflection in 2020 where the introduction of bills doubled from the previous year. Notably, these bills are not limited to the sports and bathroom bills that are well-known in mainstream media. Both types of legislation restrict the movement of trans people; bathroom bills require that individuals use the restroom that corresponds with their sex-linked biology (i.e., someone assigned a male sex at birth is required to use a male/men’s bathroom), and sports bills restrict individuals from playing on sports teams in schools that do not align with their sex-linked biology.(Fischer, 2023; Murib, 2020) Bathroom bills and sports legislation represented less than 14% of introduced bills in 2024 and about a quarter of all bills introduced between 2015 and 2016(2024 Anti-Trans Bills, n.d.) (Fig. 1).

Bills targeting access to various forms of healthcare and education-related bills have had the greatest increase in growth, resulting in a public health crisis for trans populations across the US (Fig. 1). A cultural crossroads endemic of the political polarization around human rights has profound health implications. There is a dearth of research that conceptualizes the patterns of these anti-trans bills, bills that are protective for trans people, and bills that are either discriminatory or protective for individuals of color as they exist in the same time and space. Further, much of the health policy research conceptualizing state environments as exposures to adverse outcomes does not provide a gendered racial analysis of the immense impact of the combination of anti-trans and racist policies that have been introduced and/or enacted over the past decade.

From 2015 to 2024, state legislatures were more active than the federal government branches in enacting policies that directly impact the lives of trans people. This may be in part due to congressional inaction and the limited effectiveness of policymaking around gender identity at the federal level; several attempts at passing anti-discrimination, anti-bullying, and other protections have stalled in Congress. (Rep. Cicilline, 2019; Sen. Casey, 2021) State legislatures are therefore at the forefront of defining trans rights policymaking.(Mezey, 2020) A recent analysis posited that states with more harmful policy environments for trans individuals engaged in one or more of three distinct actions: evading Obama-era administration anti-discrimination efforts with legal battles in federal courts, restricting local city and township ordinances that looked to expand anti-discrimination policies and laws to include sexual orientation, and gender identity, and/or the 2016–2020 Trump administration increasing states’ autonomy over trans-related policymaking by rolling back Obama-era anti-discrimination policies.(Mezey, 2020) As the second Trump administration begins to enact federal anti-trans policies, most notably a decision that the US government would only recognize two sexes (female and male), and these sexes are to be defined as “biological sex”, states may additionally be primed to promote anti-trans state

policies or roll back existing protections, as has happened in Iowa.(Boso, 2025; Iowa Governor Signs Bill Removing Gender Identity from State Civil Rights Protections, 2025; Medina et al., n.d.)

As anti-trans policies have increased throughout the US, trans health research has begun to focus on the health impacts of the policies that are intended to harm trans individuals.(Hughto et al., 2022; Kline et al., 2023; Miller-Jacobs et al., 2023; Tran et al., 2023) More specifically, mapping and modeling inclusive/exclusionary or protective/harmful political environments at the state level has become more common. Various methods, including legal epidemiology,(Burris et al., 2002, 2020; Ramanathan et al., 2017) have been used to calculate inclusive (i.e., legal name change protections) or exclusionary policies (i.e., religious exemptions for businesses) and mark them as political determinants of health, a needed theoretical addition to the literature surrounding trans health and state-level policy exposures.(Kline et al., 2023) Some studies found that exclusionary laws largely focused on the criminalization of trans identities, while inclusionary laws focused on access to services through government agencies (i.e., access to Medicare/Medicaid, housing, etc.).(Kline et al., 2023; Mezey, 2019) These same studies have emphasized that political determinants of health at the state level in the US may advance or restrict health equity among trans individuals, emphasizing it is important to evaluate anti- and protective trans policies that directly impact healthcare access, as these policies have immense impacts on the health of trans people.

While the theoretical turn to focus on political determinants of health and power at the state level has greatly enhanced the field of trans health, there are still opportunities to investigate how state-level policies impact trans people of color not only based on the axis of their trans experiences but also as people of color who are impacted by state-level policies relevant to structural racism.(Wesp et al., 2019; Zubizarreta et al., 2024; Zubizarreta & Beccia, 2025) Power is a key driver of health for trans people of color. As identified in Fung’s Levels of Power, values and norms are a specific ethical power that influences structural power, covering policies, and everyday displays of power.(Fung, 2020) These are greatly intertwined with how gender discourse configures power in the US, a country shaped and reshaped by anti-Indigenous, anti-Black, and cissexist (an ideology that cisgender people’s gender experiences are more “natural” or “normal” than trans people’s experiences) ideals. Analyses that focus on policy climate assume the experiences of trans individuals are affected only by policies that explicitly impact expressions of gender, devoid of racial implications for trans individuals of color. When comparing analyses that categorize the level of structural racism across states to those that categorize trans-related laws across the states, there are several discrepancies in what is deemed a “safer” state for people of color compared to what is deemed a “safer” state for trans people. For instance, a recent study classifying state-level structural racism and its impact on health found that several Northeastern states (i.e., Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts) were categorized as Mostly Harmful or Mixed for people of color. Widely used trans-rights policy trackers like the Movement Advancement Project, label these same states as highly protective for trans people. This discordance could lead to policy advocates focusing less on these states, leaving behind trans people of color who likely have very different experiences than their white counterparts.

To consider that one state is “safer” than another state for trans individuals provides an incomplete understanding of the political climate for trans individuals of color who experience oppression on multiple axes of power from dominant systems.(Galupo & and Orphanidys, 2022; Griffin, 2016; Lacombe- Duncan et al., 2022) Some studies that do include implications for trans individuals of color do not include race in their definition and conceptualization of the state-policy environment and are only looking at trans-related policies.(Du Bois et al., 2018; Goldenberg et al., 2020) Most studies investigate the relationship between race and a health outcome post hoc and use policies relevant to trans rights as the marker for state-level exposure. There is opportunity and necessity to focus on the definition of statelevel policy exposure as multi-faceted for trans individuals of color. A recent study with US trans women conceptualized their analysis to look at healthcare access as an outcome that would be associated with the health of all participants, while policies that focus on equality (e.g., nondiscrimination) would only be associated with better health for white trans women.(King et al., 2024) These decisions in study design allow for more intentional, critical, and impactful health research for trans individuals of color by explicitly outlining which policies and mechanisms differentially impact trans individuals of different races/ethnicities.

Anti-trans legislation passed in state legislatures may be related to the political ideology that is dominant and/or the amount of ideological diversity that is present in a specific state legislative body. Political polarization within and across states is important to monitor in relation to population health.(Krieger et al., 2024) Mapping the state legislature ideology and the ideological diversity therein may give insights into where there are opportunities to advocate against anti-trans legislation; even within more conservative/state legislative bodies. For instance, knowing if a state’s legislature has a more liberal ideology, overall, may be associated with passing more protective policies as opposed to more harmful policies.

This study aimed to identify alternative ways of defining state-level policy exposures that are relevant for trans people of color in the US. These typologies of states are intended to be useful as policy exposures that can be applied to datasets that include or focus on the health, disease, and well-being experiences of trans individuals of color in the US.

## 2. Study Data and Methods

This study used data from the Movement Advancement Project (MAP) in September 2024 to ascertain indicators related to trans experience in the US, a published account of structural racism categories across the US in 2013, and a measure of state legislator voting behaviors from 2013 to 2018.(Agénor et al., 2021; Jahn et al., 2023; Movement Advancement Project | Snapshot, n.d.; Shor & McCARTY, 2011) The MAP and structural racism indicators were used to create a typology of states that consider both trans policies (MAP) and racial policies (structural racism categories) that impact trans people of color. The state legislature voting behaviors data was used post-hoc to determine associations between class state typology (level of harmfulness/protectiveness), political-ideological trends in state legislatures from 2013–2018, and ideological diversity in those state legislatures in 2018.

### 2.1 Description of Data Sources and Measures

### 2.1.1 State-level policy indicators: manifest variables

Anti-trans and protective policies as of September 2024: MAP is an independent non-profit think tank that creates measures and US map visuals of LGBTQ+ equality and election and voting-related laws, and tracks the number of protective and harmful trans bills in the US that have been passed at the state-level through September 2024.(MAP, 2022) The major categories of laws covered by the “Gender Identity Tally” from MAP include: “Bans on transgender youth sports participation,” “Safe schools: school nondiscrimination,” “Safe schools: anti-bullying,” “Bans on medical care for transgender youth,” “Bans on insurance exclusions of transgender-related care,” “Hate crime laws,” “Gay/trans panic defense bans,” “Restrictions on name changes,” “Name change process,” “Changing gender marker on driver’s licenses,” “Changing gender marker on birth certificates,” and “Gender neutral markers.” MAP assigns a point value to each policy; harmful and discriminatory policies are given negative points and protective and inclusive policies are given positive points. States receive points between 0 and 1 when only a part of a protective law has been enacted or policies only impact a subset of the state (e.g., local ordinances that protect gender identity). Points are summed to yield a policy tally for each state. There are a total of 22 points available to states. Gender Identity Tallies for each state are further categorized as:

1. Negative protection (harmful and discriminatory): less than 0 points 2. Low protection: 0 to 5.25 points; 0-24.9% of total possible Gender Identity Tally points 3. Fair protection: 5.5 to 10.75 points; 25-49.9% of total Gender Identity Tally points 4. Medium protection: 11 to 16.25 points; 50-74.9% of total Gender Identity Tally points 5. High protection: 16.5 + points; 75–100% of total Gender Identity Tally points

For our analysis, we deconstructed the overall MAP Gender Identity tally into the categories of relationship recognition, non-discrimination, religious exemptions, LGBT youth, healthcare, criminal justice, and ID documents. MAP indicators are continuous; we created categorical variables for these continuous indicators and created cut points. All negative values were assigned 0, and all positive values were divided into four quartiles. For some manifest indicators, there was not enough variability in the data to create four distinct positive quartiles. For instance, the non-discrimination variable has 75th and 100th percentiles that overlap; thus, we combined these into one cut-point within the non-discrimination variable.

Structural racism legal database: Policies from 2013: Recently, public health and legal scholars developed a database that accounted for 10 legal domains related to structural racism, with 78 specific policies/laws.(Agénor et al., 2021) These domains cover both harmful laws (i.e., discriminating against marginalized racial/ethnic groups) and protective laws (i.e., preventing the unjust treatment of individuals from marginalized racial/ethnic populations) from 2010 to 2013. For this research, we use the state regional patterning of latent classes of state-structural racism-related laws from 2013

<!-- Page 7 -->


conceived by Jahn et al. (2023): mostly protective, mostly harmful, and mixed. This structural racism measure also considered earned income tax credit policies across the US.

State legislature voting record and ideological diversity: Changes from 1993 to 2018: The Shor-McCarty state legislator ideology data provides an estimation of state legislator voting behavior based on legislators’ ideological positioning from voting roll calls and Project Vote Smart’s National Political Awareness Test (NPAT).(Shor & McCARTY, 2011) The NPAT compares legislators across time and states on a common ideological scale–as legislators who are being compared across states are voting on different measures from one another. The use of the NPAT allows for standardization to be able to compare legislator behaviors and thereby state legislatures across states. Using the means and standard deviations of NPAT scores, we created trajectories to model changes in state legislature ideology between 1993 and 2018 and whether ideological diversity changed over the same period (Fig. 2).

Mean values of NPAT scores range from − 1 to 1; greater mean values indicate a more conservative legislature. Greater standard deviation (SD) values indicate more ideological diversity in state legislatures (inclusive of House and Senate chambers). Figure 1 depicts mean values on the y-axis, years on the x-axis, and a color gradient is used to depict the SD value at each point. Deeper saturation indicates less ideological diversity at that time point(s).

## 3. Analytic Methods

### 3.1 Polytomous latent class analysis with policies specific to transgender and Black individuals

We used a polytomous (multiple categorical indicators) latent class analysis to identify patterns in state policies among US states. Latent class analysis, compared to other statistical techniques with clustered data, allows for a variety of metrics to assess model fit and the appropriate number of latent classes. The number of classes can be selected for reasonings including theoretical or parsimony/model fit.

Given the theoretical nature of the research inquiry, we provide the parsimony criteria (BIC, AIC, G2), and consider theoretical justification as a primary factor in determining the number of classes.(Linzer & Lewis, 2011) This approach allows for the selected model to not only fit the data well but also aligns with our conceptualization of state-level policy environments as complex and multi-faceted for trans individuals of color in the US. Classes were assigned using the poLCA software package in R. The package uses “expectation-maximization to find maximum likelihood estimates of the model parameters”.(Linzer & Lewis, 2011) 3.2 One-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) testing; political ideology and ideological diversity

To assess whether there are differences in political ideology and ideological diversity across state legislatures in our latent classes, we conducted a one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). This was an appropriate method as it assesses differences in the continuous political variables across class membership. Given a significant ANOVA result for political ideology and class membership, a Tukey’s Honest Significant Difference (HSD) post-hoc test was performed to identify specific differences between all three classes.

## 5. Discussion

This is one of the first studies to consider the exposure of US state policies that are defined by both structural racism and anti-trans policies and further examines the political makeup of legislative bodies across states. Political, social, and cultural geography begets policies that contribute to the multifaceted ways that the health of trans individuals of color is impacted. Further, the past decade has brought about an extraordinary amount of legislation that reflects white supremacy and anti-trans rhetoric in the US, with various states implementing discriminatory or protective laws that impact trans individuals of color.(Galupo & and Orphanidys, 2022; King et al., 2024; Krieger et al., 2024) We find that state legislatures with more liberal political ideology are associated with more protectiveness for trans people, compared to mixed and mostly harmful states. The amount of ideological diversity in state legislatures was not associated with the level of protectiveness in our latent classes, suggesting that even more conservative state legislatures with higher ideological diversity among legislators are not associated with more protectiveness. However, as we found in developing the latent classes, even the Mostly Protective class contained states that were negative or mixed in the structural racism indicator, emblematic of the degree of harmfulness experienced by people of color broadly in the US.

### 5.1 Policy differences across latent classes: hate crime laws

The current study found that Mostly Protective states were marked by several differences compared to mixed and mostly harmful states. One of the more notable distinctions was that protective criminal justice policies relevant to trans individuals only exist in states classified as mostly protective. No protective criminal justice policies related to trans individuals exist in the mixed or mostly harmful states. MAP defines the criminal justice domain in their data as: (1) Specifically enumerating crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity, (2) Data collection related to crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and (3) Required training for law enforcement related to sexual orientation or gender identity. This study used the first criteria of “specifically enumerating crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity” as an indicator of protective policies for trans individuals related to criminal justice. As such, only mostly protective states, per our latent class analysis, have hate crime laws should trans individuals be harmed based on their transgender or nonbinary identity.

Our findings around hate crime laws are crucial to contextualizing health for trans individuals of color in the US. Evidence shows that in states with hate crime protections for trans individuals, adverse health outcomes such as suicidality and mood disorders are less prevalent compared to states without those protections.(Cramer et al., 2025) Yet, hate crime laws are contentious among marginalized groups. While there is convergence among policymakers, civil rights groups, and impacted communities that measures to prevent hate crimes are needed, they disagree on the value of hate crime laws and typical criminal justice system responses to them (e.g., incarceration).(Sinnar, 2022) Additionally, hate crime protections are only guaranteed to US citizens, leaving undocumented and immigrant trans individuals of color without protection. Although most criminal prosecutions occur at the state level, creating 50 different

systems, most follow the same restrictions outlined in the US Constitution. This results in more similarities than differences in the systems but does not mean that hate crime protections are identical across the states that do have them. 5.2 Policy differences across latent classes: Healthcare protections

Healthcare protections were another policy domain with a similar pattern as criminal justice policies, but in this case, only the Mostly Harmful latent class contained states with discriminatory laws. Defined by MAP as the existence of private insurance non-discrimination laws based on gender identity and bans on insurance exclusions of trans-related healthcare, the mostly harmful states either had no law providing trans-inclusive insurance protections or had laws that explicitly permit insurers to refuse to cover genderaffirming care. 5.3 Policy differences across latent classes: Structural racism indicator

All three classes in our trans and race state policy analysis contain states considered “mostly harmful” by the structural racism indicator.(Jahn et al., 2023) This further emphasizes the importance of being critical of the state typologies found in recent efforts to mark states as “inclusive” or “protective”, as these may not accurately define policy environments for trans people of color impacted by laws related to structural racism in addition to transgender-related policies.(Du Bois et al., 2018; Kline et al., 2023; Miller-Jacobs et al., 2023) In our study, there were four states (Delaware, Hawaii, New Hampshire, and Virginia) in the Mostly Protective class that also were categorized as “mostly harmful” based on the structural racism indicator, and four states (Maine, Massachusetts, Nevada, and Vermont) in the Mostly Protective class that were categorized as “mixed” using the structural racism indicator. Our findings suggest that selective protection may outline specific rights in trans policymaking where states still fail to address protections for trans individuals of color, specifically.

There were two states in our analysis that were in the Mostly Harmful class that were categorized as “mostly protective” using the Jahn et. al structural racism indicator: Nebraska and Utah. Nebraska has a history of state-government actions that likely created supportive and protective policies for people of color in the state. For example, Nebraska was the first state to establish an agency dedicated to the advancement and advocacy of Latiné individuals. Established in 1972, it was estimated that 30,000 Mexican Americans lived in Nebraska.(The Nebraska Commission on Latino-Affairs Works on Growing Its Impact despite Potential Challenges, n.d.) In 2021, the Nebraska state legislature amended the Nebraska Fair Employment Practices Act and expanded the definition of protections for race to include “protection against discrimination for characteristics such as skin color, hair texture, and protective hairstyles.”(“Natural Hair Protections,” n.d.) In states like Nebraska and Utah, some protections prohibit discrimination based on race/ethnicity, but far fewer, if not non-existent, legal protections for trans individuals exist in those states. Additionally, it is not only the absence of protective laws but the presence of harmful laws that impact trans individuals in these two states. Utah and Nebraska have

numerous state bans that are similar, including laws prohibiting trans individuals from using bathrooms or facilities consistent with their gender in government buildings, and targeted religious exemption laws. (Medina et al., n.d.; Movement Advancement Project | Snapshot, n.d.) The bathroom bans define “sex” to exclude trans individuals, similar to the Trump administration’s policy that there are two sexes, male and female, that are biologically determined from birth and not changeable. Healthcare laws and policies are particularly harmful in both states, banning gender-affirming care for trans youth and adults in their state Medicaid policies. 5.4 State legislature political ideology and ideological diversity across latent classes

State legislature political ideology and latent class membership were associated in our study. Mostly Protective states were more likely to have a more “liberal” political ideology within the state legislature, which was associated with policies that would benefit trans individuals and individuals of color (Table 4). The political ideology of the state legislature often predicts the ideology of the state residents, as they voted the legislators into office.(Krieger et al., 2024) However, as we found, class membership in the Mostly Protective category still included eight states that were mixed or mostly harmful when looking at the structural racism classifications only. As the state legislature likely reflects the political ideology of the state’s constituents, these “liberal havens” for trans individuals do not appear to show the same protectiveness for trans individuals of color. Regional patterning of these states illustrates that while states in the northeastern US are commonly seen as more protective for trans individuals,(Kline et al., 2023; MAP, 2022) our results and other studies have found that these states are less than protective for trans individuals of color.(Jahn et al., 2023; Veazie et al., 2025)

## 6. Implications

Advocacy for health equity for trans people, people of color, and those at the intersections is pivotal in the current US political and cultural climate. Our study showcases how state legislatures fared in protecting trans people of color preceding the second Trump administration, an administration that within the first 100 days has rolled back protections and rights for marginalized groups, priming states like Iowa to also take measures to restrict trans rights. It is even more imperative that researchers conceptualize and measure state-level policy measures as they pertain to not only trans-related laws but also laws that are concerned with structural racism, as several states that are deemed protective overall in our study were considered less protective for people of color. Further, in our latent class analysis Nebraska and Utah were classified as Mostly Harmful, but in the structural racism indicator were mostly protective for people of color. These two states show that while knowing the political ideology of the state legislature is associated with protectiveness or harmfulness, the passage of harmful trans-related policies in specific states is driven by the legislating and advocacy done in those legislatures. In states where there are mixed or mostly protective structural racism policies, there may be opportunities to advocate for the well-being of trans individuals as individuals who are also impacted by structural oppression and build coalitions across issues of identity-based marginalization. In all, our

## 7. Limitations, Conclusions, and Future Directions

Our study is not without limitations. We used pre-existing definitions for manifest policy indicators from two different sources that are intended to be stand-alone measures. There is a possibility that information that is provided by any singular source is hidden by combining these measures. For instance, while several states in the northeastern US score as “Mixed” or “Mostly Harmful” using the Jahn et. al (2013) typology for structural racism, our latent class analysis found these are still more protective for trans individuals of color, which is more line with the MAP classifications of these states. Further, as we find that policy exposures need a more nuanced definition to be relevant to trans individuals of color, several racial and/or ethnic groups may still be impacted differentially by structural racism in the US. Future research would require measures of Anti-Black racism at the state policy level, for instance, to more accurately define the state political environment for Black trans individuals.

While there are considerations for how the latent class analysis was conceptualized and a need for racial/ethnic group specificity in defining structural racism, this is one of the first studies to attempt to define policy exposures for trans individuals of color at the state level and find associations with statelegislature political ideology.
